pedagogy_description: How PyDA Course teaches programming and data analysis: the lesson loop, the math-first derivations, the short lessons, and the game layer, explained for teachers and students.
pedagogy_intro_1: This course was built on one question: how does a beginner actually learn to program? The answer shapes every lesson, every quiz, and every point on the progress bar.
pedagogy_intro_2: This page explains the design in plain terms, so teachers can see what is happening under the hood, and so can students. Nothing here happens behind their back.
pedagogy_core_lede: Every lesson runs the same loop that working programmers live in: meet a problem, derive a tool, run it, then check what stuck.
pedagogy_core_hook: A hook, often mathematical. Each lesson opens from a concrete pattern you already half-know: an arithmetic sequence, a function rule, a set. It is a place to stand.
pedagogy_core_derive: Concepts are built step by step in prose and code, nothing is asserted before it is earned, so the 'why' is never an afterthought.
pedagogy_core_run: Code you can run immediately. Every code snippet executes in the browser. There is no wall between reading and doing, and running is a click, never a setup.
pedagogy_core_check: A check that costs nothing. Each lesson ends with a low-stakes quiz with instant feedback, plus challenges that reward working the answer out before revealing it.
pedagogy_anatomy_lede: Open any lesson and you will meet the same five moves, in the same order:
pedagogy_anatomy_1: Narrative sections that derive each idea step by step before naming it.
pedagogy_anatomy_2: Short, runnable examples that show the idea working. Every one of them executes.
pedagogy_anatomy_3: 🧩 Challenges: think first, then reveal. The answer stays folded until you have actually tried.
pedagogy_anatomy_4: Socratic questions that ask you to re-derive the idea rather than recall it.
pedagogy_anatomy_5: A quick-check quiz with instant, judgment-free feedback.
pedagogy_short_lede: Short lessons are deliberate. Each lasts around fifteen minutes, because knowledge sticks better in small, regular doses than in rare marathon sessions.
pedagogy_short_1: One concept per lesson. Each lesson teaches one idea deeply instead of five ideas shallowly.
pedagogy_short_2: Fifteen minutes fits a daily habit. Short enough to finish, short enough to repeat tomorrow, which is exactly the rhythm the streak system encourages.
pedagogy_short_3: Frequent beats long. Five short returns build more durable knowledge than one marathon sitting.
pedagogy_short_4: Depth is a spiral. Ideas first met in a short lesson return in richer form in later lessons, modules, and projects.
pedagogy_spiral_lede: The course is a spiral curriculum: you meet an idea, revisit it with more depth, and finally use it in something real.
pedagogy_spiral_py: Python 101, the foundation: printing and variables, then operators, control flow, functions, strings, data structures, and file I/O. Each short lesson builds directly on the last.
pedagogy_spiral_da: Data Analysis with real data in pandas: Series and DataFrames, selection and filtering, cleaning, group-by, and a complete Titanic exploration.
pedagogy_spiral_projects: Guided projects. Each one reuses earlier skills in a realistic build, so the spiral closes with practice instead of repetition.
pedagogy_math_lede: PyDA stands for Python + Data Analysis, but the glue between them is mathematical thinking. The lessons borrow mathematicians' most useful notations, so that programming becomes applied math literacy:
pedagogy_math_1: Sequences ↔ loops. range(n) is the arithmetic progression a, a+d, a+2d, …
pedagogy_math_2: Functions ↔ Python functions. f(x) = x² − 5x + 6 is a rule on parameters, and add(a, b) is the same idea in code.
pedagogy_math_3: Set-builder notation ↔ comprehensions. {x² | x ∈ {1,2,3}} is almost literal Python.
pedagogy_math_4: Half-open intervals ↔ slicing. s[a:b] behaves exactly like the interval [a, b), and there is a reason: it makes slices compose cleanly.
pedagogy_assess_lede: Quizzes are formative. A wrong answer costs nothing, it only feeds a game-style 'death' in your report. Instant feedback shows the right reasoning on the spot, so a mistake becomes the moment you learn instead of a reason to fear the quiz.
pedagogy_game_lede: XP, ranks, streaks, and quests exist for one reason: motivation. The design follows the evidence in
pedagogy_game_post: (a visual-novel-based computing course measured with N-Gain 0.61 and 87.6% acceptance).
pedagogy_game_body: Numbers only ever accumulate, so nothing can be lost. The game rewards effort without punishing mistakes. XP is earned for any visible action: running code, finishing a lesson, a correct quiz answer, or simply returning on a new day.
pedagogy_growth_lede: The progress page is an exercise in reading your own learning: win rate, K/D/A, farm, streaks, consistency, and diagnostics including an N-Gain equivalent. It is a mirror for self-regulation.
pedagogy_ecology_heading: Where skill comes from: the ecology of talent
pedagogy_ecology_lede: Skill grows inside environments, places where people watch good models, make mistakes on purpose, and get invited to join in. Daniel Coyle's work on deep practice, ignition, and culture shows what makes such environments work. This course applies it feature by feature. Here are the ideas and where each one shows up:
pedagogy_ecology_1: Mistakes are information. Deep practice means feeling the error and reaching again. Every quick check, quiz, and challenge is a low-stakes attempt with instant feedback, tuned so you miss around 20% of the time, the documented sweet spot for learning.
pedagogy_ecology_2: Watch, struggle, borrow. Lessons start with worked examples to study closely, then make you re-derive and rebuild the same idea. Borrowing a pattern you just saw is how working craftsmen learn, and it is encouraged here.
pedagogy_ecology_3: Motivation starts with an invitation. XP, streaks, ranks, and badges are the pull that draws you in. Guided projects and capstones show a possible future self, the horizon that says: if they can do it, why can't I?
pedagogy_ecology_4: The workshop model. Fundamentals are built piece by piece before serious performance, and projects put you to work on real builds. The progress page is the floor plan of the workshop, what is solid and what needs another pass.
pedagogy_privacy_lede: Everything stays in the browser's local storage under a single key. There is no account, no server, and no leaderboard. No data ever leaves the device, which makes the course safe to run in a classroom with zero setup.
pedagogy_teacher_lede: Running the course takes five minutes and a projector:
pedagogy_teacher_1: Assign a path. Python 101 first, then Data Analysis. The learner’s progress page is the class map.
pedagogy_teacher_2: Teach live from the lessons. Every example runs in the browser, so a lesson can become a live demo at any moment.
pedagogy_teacher_3: Use the guided projects as deliverables. Each is a complete, gradeable build, not an exercise.
pedagogy_teacher_4: Treat quizzes as formative. Read their accuracy as a signal of coverage, not as a grade to collect.
pedagogy_guide_link_lede: Why lessons are short, the lesson loop, and the thinking behind the game layer.

guide_description: A step-by-step guide to writing a real-world project for this course and opening your first pull request.
guide_intro: Every real-world project here started as one markdown file in someone's pull request. This page lists exactly what to change, in order, plus the commands to check your work before you submit it.
guide_step_1_body: Use Node 22.23.4 or newer, as package.json requires, plus git. The included .nvmrc selects 22.23.4 when you use nvm.
guide_step_1_steps:
Run the commands below to install the pinned Node version with nvm and select it.
Check Node and git before continuing.
Without nvm, install Node 22.23.4 or newer from nodejs.org and reopen your terminal.
guide_step_1_expect:
v22.23.4  # or a newer compatible version
git version 2.39.5  # any recent git version is fine
guide_step_2_title: Fork if you need your own copy
guide_step_2_body: External contributors work in a fork and push branches there. If you own the repository, work directly from upstream; forking is unnecessary.
guide_step_2_steps:
Repository owner? Skip to the next step and clone upstream.
Otherwise open github.com/abderrahim-lectures/python-data-analysis-course and choose Fork.
Select your GitHub account as the destination and wait for the copy to finish.
guide_step_2_expect:
For a fork: github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/python-data-analysis-course
For an owner: use the original repository and continue below.
guide_step_3_body: Cloning downloads the repository to your computer. Install the exact package versions in the lock file before editing or running anything.
guide_step_3_steps:
Clone the fork URL if you made one; an owner can use the upstream URL below.
Move into the repository and run npm install.
Allow time for the roughly 485 dependency packages; the exact count and download time can change.
guide_step_3_expect:
Cloning into 'python-data-analysis-course'...
added 485 packages in ...  # approximate count; your time will vary
You are now in the python-data-analysis-course directory.
guide_step_4_title: Check the slug, then create a branch
guide_step_4_body: Check the existing project filenames first: file-organizer.md already exists. The grade calculator in templates/ is a worked example, not a project published in src/content/projects. Choose a new lowercase hyphenated slug that does not appear in any of the four locale directories.
guide_step_4_steps:
Search the existing Markdown filenames in src/content/projects/ before creating a file.
Read the short beginner project file-organizer.md. Keep ai-agent.md as an optional longer reference.
Choose another slug if yours is already present in any of the four language directories.
Create a branch named for your chosen slug. The placeholder below shows the pattern; replace it before running the commands.
guide_step_4_expect:
ls src/content/projects/file-organizer.md prints the existing path.
A new branch is active, and your chosen slug is absent from all existing project directories.
guide_step_5_body: Copy templates/project.md to your English project path. It provides the guided-project structure: setup, short runnable steps, expected output, troubleshooting, checkpoints, and a recap.
guide_step_5_steps:
Open templates/project.md and copy its structure: standard-library setup, short runnable steps, expected output, troubleshooting, checkpoints, pitfalls, and a Credit and licence section.
Read `file-organizer.md` for another real example of scope and tone; `ai-agent.md` is an optional longer reference.
Replace the sample calculator and every authoring comment with your own project, and run every command you document.
Replace the placeholders `YOUR-SLUG` and `your-id` everywhere before you open the pull request.
guide_step_5_expect:
Your new English Markdown file exists, with your own project title replacing the template example.
The full template remains at templates/project.md for reference.
guide_step_6_body: English frontmatter needs title, description, and difficulty. Add your contributor id as author only there. Arabic, Spanish, and French use title, description, and difficulty, with no author field.
guide_step_6_steps:
Write a specific title and a short description in each language.
Translate title and description, optional tags, and prerequisites for your learners. Keep schema keys, technology names, and code identifiers consistent.
Keep difficulty exactly as the schema enum demands in src/content.config.ts: beginner, intermediate, or advanced in every language; do not translate it.
Set author to your existing contributor id, or a new id you will register in step 9, only on the English entry. Localized pages inherit authorship from English.
guide_step_6_translation: For localized frontmatter, translate title and description into the learner’s language. Preserve the exact English difficulty enum, and omit author because English supplies authorship.
guide_step_6_expect:
Every language entry has title, description, and difficulty.
Only src/content/projects/<your-slug>.md has an author field.
guide_step_7_body: Tests require the same project in English, Arabic, Spanish, and French. Arabic is required too. Use the same English filename in all four locations, including the required ar directory.
guide_step_7_steps:
Create your English project file, then add the same unused filename under src/content/projects/ar/<your-slug>.md, es/<your-slug>.md, and fr/<your-slug>.md. Tests expect all four languages.
The template project.translated.md supplies the full teaching outline, not just minimal frontmatter: translate its title, description, learner-facing prose, expected outcomes, troubleshooting, and checkpoints for every locale.
Translate textual metadata and headings, but preserve the exact enum difficulty (beginner/intermediate/advanced) required by src/content.config.ts. Omit author here.
Keep runnable commands and expected outputs in agreement, and retain accepted Step, Paso, Étape, and الخطوة step prefixes. Each row in the list becomes a new subscriber-visible learner instruction after editing is complete.
guide_step_7_expect:
src/content/projects/<your-slug>.md
src/content/projects/ar/<your-slug>.md
src/content/projects/es/<your-slug>.md
src/content/projects/fr/<your-slug>.md
All four files exist and are translated.
guide_step_8_body: Include an `examples/<your-slug>/` folder with the runnable code and a notebook. Every project page shows Colab, Kaggle, and Binder badges, so the notebook those links point at has to exist.
guide_step_8_steps:
Create `examples/<your-slug>/` with the code your lesson explains and a README. `templates/example-README.md` is a starting copy that includes the required credit and licence block.
Add `notebook.ipynb` mirroring the steps. `node scripts/generate-notebooks.mjs` generates a missing English notebook and the `notebook.{ar,es,fr}.ipynb` twins from each locale’s Markdown, so run it once the prose is final and commit the results.
Point the Colab, Kaggle, and Binder links under “Where to run this” at those notebooks: English at `notebook.ipynb`, each translation at its own `notebook.<locale>.ipynb`.
Add `pyproject.toml` when the project uses uv, and replace `YOUR-SLUG` and `your-id` in every file and badge URL.
guide_step_8_expect:
examples/<your-slug>/README.md
examples/<your-slug>/grades.py  # your chosen filename
examples/<your-slug>/notebook.ipynb
examples/<your-slug>/notebook.{ar,es,fr}.ipynb  # generated
examples/<your-slug>/pyproject.toml  # when using uv
guide_step_9_body: Author credit comes from src/lib/contributors.ts, not git history. Search the existing IDs before adding another entry. Reuse yours if it is already registered.
guide_step_9_steps:
Open src/lib/contributors.ts and read the id values in CONTRIBUTORS.
If your id exists, use it unchanged in the English project's author field.
If you are new, add one entry with a unique lowercase hyphenated id, your name, and optionally your GitHub handle.
Duplicate IDs fail the tests. Do not put author in any translated project file.
guide_step_9_expect:
The English author's id exactly matches one registered id.
Existing entries remain intact and no duplicate id was added.
guide_step_10_title: Build before running tests and TypeScript
guide_step_10_body: Run npm run build first on a fresh checkout. It generates Paraglide localization files; tests and TypeScript need those modules. It also regenerates projectSlugs.data.json from your translations.
guide_step_10_steps:
npm run build generates src/paraglide/messages.js and runtime.js, then builds every page.
The first build downloads about 138 MB of Pyodide assets; later builds reuse existing files and need less setup time.
Run npm run test and npx tsc --noEmit after the successful build. Commit the generated src/lib/projectSlugs.data.json changes.
guide_step_10_expect:
Build finishes with no failed pages and updated slug data.
Then run the tests and TypeScript, whose commands require the generated Paraglide modules.
guide_step_11_body: Run npm run dev from the repository root. Astro says which local address it uses, normally http://localhost:4321/. Open the contributor guide and your project page to inspect the actual content.
guide_step_11_steps:
Check the English page and its Arabic, Spanish, and French versions, including links and code blocks.
Use http://localhost:4321/contributors-guide/ to inspect your own working copy of this guide.
If a slug or page is missing, stop, correct it, and keep the terminal open while the server runs.
Let the initial content indexing finish; a fresh checkout can take longer than it looks at first.
guide_step_11_expect:
The Astro terminal prints a Local URL, normally http://localhost:4321/.
Your project loads in each language at the localized address shown by your local site.
guide_step_12_title: Read the test results before submitting
guide_step_12_body: A green result records the last verification. Review and merge are separate steps, so passing checks alone never submits or publishes the project. Read any failure beside its expected and received output, fix it, and rerun the checks.
guide_step_12_steps:
A reported run on 2026-11-19 passed 1790 tests across 42 files; repository growth will change that total, so this records a historical result.
Use the actual test total in your own terminal, not this stale sample value.
Successful local commands check source files; they do not submit, review, or publish your project.
Include your own results in the pull request and resolve failures before asking for review.
guide_step_12_expect:
Historical example: 1790 tests across 42 files passed on 2026-11-19.
Always use your terminal’s current totals.
A green check is local verification; publication happens after review, merge, and deployment.
guide_step_13_body: Review the intended file list after staging. Include the companion examples if present, all four Markdown entries, your registry change if new, and the generated src/lib/projectSlugs.data.json.
guide_step_13_steps:
Run git status --short before git add -A to inspect your changes.
Stage intentionally, then run git status --short again to verify that all four language files and generated slug data are listed.
Commit only the files for this project, then push the branch to your fork or upstream if you are the owner.
Keep your PR description clear about passing local checks and the remaining review step.
Do not commit node_modules, public/pyodide, local server state, credentials, or unrelated changes.
guide_step_13_expect:
git status lists everything intended for this one project.
Check the four language entries, optional examples, registry edit if needed, projectSlugs.data.json, and any new site messages for this contribution.
guide_step_14_title: Open the pull request and understand publication
guide_step_14_body: Open a pull request against upstream main, describe what the project teaches, and list the checks you ran. Local build, preview, test, and push commands do not publish a project; merging the pull request publishes all four project pages together.
guide_step_14_steps:
Open GitHub and choose Compare & pull request for the branch you pushed.
Describe the project, its intended learner, and your build/test/typecheck results; reviewers assess the content as well as the commands.
Check that the final Credit and licence section names you as author with your contributor id and keeps the CC BY 4.0 and MIT lines.
Wait for review and address requested changes before merging. There is no draft flag.
Merging to main triggers deployment, so every submitted language version goes live together.
guide_step_14_expect:
An open pull request with your changes and review status.
Publication happens after merge and deployment, not after the guide commands alone.

guide_refs_description: The books the Statistics 101 section is built from, with what each one covers and which lessons it is best for.
guide_refs_link_lede: Five books, and what each one is best for
guide_refs_intro: Every lesson in this section is written from standard sources rather than invented. These are the books behind it, and what each one is genuinely useful for — so when a lesson leaves you wanting more on one topic, you know which to open.
guide_refs_foot: All five are standard undergraduate or practitioner texts. The lesson pages do not cite them inline: the goal is that you can read a lesson without a book open, and reach for one only when you want to go further.
guide_ref_kaptein: The closest match to this course’s approach: statistics as something you do in code. Its chapter on correlation and resampling is the clearest treatment of the topics the other books skip.
guide_ref_peck: A thorough introductory text with a large bank of worked examples. Best for the descriptive half of the course: quartiles, spread and the mechanics of the normal curve.
guide_ref_bruce: Practitioner-oriented and short on theory by design. Best for seeing each idea applied to real data, and the only one here written for people who already write code.
guide_ref_taylor: Measurement-focused and careful about the assumptions behind each technique. Denser than the others, and best once you have the basics.
guide_ref_gillard: A compact, proof-aware undergraduate treatment. Best for understanding why the formulas are what they are, rather than how to compute them.

guide_tips_heading: Things that get a pull request merged faster
guide_tip_1: Teach one thing end to end. A project that builds one small tool honestly beats one that touches five libraries.
guide_tip_2: Keep the code runnable. A reader should be able to copy a step and run it, not just read it.
guide_tip_3: Write the pitfalls section last, from the mistakes you actually made while building it.
guide_tip_4: Submit English, Arabic, Spanish, and French versions together. Use the translated template, point each locale’s badges at its own notebook, and keep the credit and licence section in every version.
guide_file_project: The required English project page. Include title, description, and difficulty, plus author with your contributor id. Follow the teaching template for the body.
guide_file_example: Companion code and a notebook that a reader can run locally or open in Colab, Kaggle, or Binder. Add a README with tested run instructions and a credit and licence block.
guide_file_registry_body: Add an entry with your id, display name, and optionally your GitHub handle. Set author: <your-id> on your project page and it appears on the contributors page.
